items.summary: In POSCO v. United States, Court No. 24-00006, filed August 8, 2025, Judge Jane A. Restani of the Court of International Trade partially sustained and partially remanded the Commerce Department's final determination in a countervailing duty administrative review of certain carbon and alloy steel cut-to-length plate from the Republic of Korea. The determination found a 0.87 percent subsidy rate for POSCO based on Korea's electricity provision and its Cap and Trade Law. The portion of the opinion provided holds that Commerce acted unreasonably in grouping the Korean steel industry with two unrelated industries in its de facto specificity analysis of the electricity subsidy.

items.summary: In this April 17, 2026 Opinion and Order, the U.S. Court of International Trade sustained in part and remanded in part the Department of Commerce's final remand redetermination in the countervailing duty administrative review of certain carbon and alloy steel cut-to-length plate from the Republic of Korea for the 2021 period of review. The court sustained Commerce's findings except the specificity finding regarding the allocation of extra Korea Allowance Units (KAUs), which it remanded. The court also noted that Commerce had found the Korean electricity subsidy was not shown to be de facto specific on remand.

items.summary: In this October 27, 2026 Opinion and Order, the U.S. Court of International Trade sustained Commerce's second remand redetermination in the same countervailing duty review of carbon and alloy steel cut-to-length plate from Korea. Commerce had determined on remand that the allocation of KAUs is de facto specific under 19 U.S.C. § 1677(5A)(D)(iii)(I), comparing 494 recipients to 906,325 companies within the Government of Korea's jurisdiction. Plaintiffs POSCO and the Government of the Republic of Korea argued that the comparison used an improper denominator, and the court sustained Commerce's determination.

items.summary: In this October 27, 2026 Opinion and Order, the U.S. Court of International Trade dismissed the complaint of pro se plaintiff Raj K. Patel for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The complaint alleged violations of international trade agreements and due-process protections related to access to certain medical technologies, and sought declaratory relief and $380 million in damages. The court denied Patel's motion to compel acceptance of the complaint as moot, finding that the cited trade agreements are not laws falling within the court's residual jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i).

items.summary: In an opinion filed October 28, 2026, the First Circuit in Wright v. United Services Automobile Association, No. 25-1979, on appeal from the District of Massachusetts, held that Massachusetts law rather than the federal filed rate doctrine governs whether policyholders may sue their motor vehicle insurers under Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 93A over rates approved by the Massachusetts Insurance Commissioner. The plaintiffs allege that the approved rates impermissibly considered income and occupation in violation of implementing regulations. The court certified the state-law questions to the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, and the excerpt provided is truncated.
items.title: Wright, et al v. United Services Automobile Association, et al

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Eighth Circuit in United States v. Kyle Ryan Cook, No. 26-1771, affirmed a sentence imposed by the Northern District of Iowa after Cook pled guilty to transmitting a communication containing a threat. The sentence was above the Guidelines range, and counsel's Anders brief challenged its substantive reasonableness. The court found no abuse of discretion, independently reviewed the record under Penson v. Ohio, found no non-frivolous issues, affirmed the judgment, and granted counsel's motion to withdraw.

items.summary: The Third Circuit denied the petition for review filed by Gurmit Singh Kahlon of a Board of Immigration Appeals decision that affirmed the denial of withholding of removal based on religion and political opinion. The court found that substantial evidence supported the finding that Gurmit Singh Kahlon did not show a clear probability of persecution if returned to India. items.summary: In a non-precedential per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit affirmed the Eastern District of Pennsylvania's grant of summary judgment to the defendants in Marquis Robinson v. Self Help Movement, et al. The court held that a supervisor's isolated requests that the plaintiff lift her back did not meet the severe or pervasive standard for hostile work environment harassment under Title VII and the PHRA. The court also held that Robinson's race-based claims concerning outside work offers and a client's racial slur were not exhausted because they fell outside the scope of his EEOC charge, and it denied his motion to file supplemental documents.

Chicago, Illinois 60604

NANCY L. MALDONADO, Circuit Judge

REBECCA TAIBLESON, Circuit
items.summary: In Kelvin Smith v. Kohler Co., et al., No. 25-3248, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal with prejudice of a pro se complaint alleging religious discrimination under Title VII based on a COVID-19 testing requirement. The court held that the amended complaint did not connect the objection to the testing requirement to a religious belief or practice, and that the district court could dismiss under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 41(b) after the plaintiff failed to file a second amended complaint as ordered. The court also held that a pro se litigant cannot represent other parties or a putative class, and that the district court acted within its discretion in declining to consider untimely and noncompliant filings.
items.title: Kelvin Smith v. Kohler Co., et al

items.summary: In Patricia Tillman v. Illinois State Board of Elections, et al., No. 26-1108, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal for failure to state a claim of a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 complaint challenging the Board's disqualification of a candidate from the March 2026 primary ballot. The court held that the plaintiff received notice and an opportunity to be heard in the Board proceedings, and that she did not plausibly allege an inadequate post-deprivation remedy because she voluntarily dismissed her state-court challenge. The court also held that the district court did not abuse its discretion by failing to order amendment sua sponte.

items.summary: In United States v. Kevin M. Cooper, No. 26-1123, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the denial of a third motion for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A). The court held that a nonretroactive change in law does not constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason under Rutherford v. United States, 146 S. Ct. 1320 (2026), and that the medical conditions and other arguments presented were insufficient to support release. The court also noted that, having found no extraordinary and compelling reason, the district court was not required to determine the extent of any reduction under the sentencing factors in 18 U.S.C. § 3553(a).

items.summary: In Calvin McMillan v. National Football League, et al., No. 26-1957, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal under 28 U.S.C. § 1915(e)(2)(B) of a copyright infringement complaint alleging that lottery ticket phrases copied lyrics from two songs about the Green Bay Packers. The court held that the plaintiff did not prove registration of the works and that the short phrases at issue, including Pack Attack, Pack Is Back, and Go Pack Go, are slogan-like combinations of ordinary words that are not protected by copyright under 37 C.F.R. § 202.1(a). The court also noted that the antitrust claims in the complaint were not pursued on appeal.

items.summary: The Seventh Circuit granted appointed counsel's motion to withdraw and dismissed the appeal of George Sisk, who pleaded guilty without a plea agreement to Hobbs Act robbery, a firearm offense under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), and felon-in-possession under § 922(g)(1). Sisk was sentenced to an aggregate 156-month prison term, and the court's order, issued under Anders v. California, found no nonfrivolous issues for appeal. The order addresses the constitutionality of § 922(g)(1), the Rule 11 plea colloquy, competency, the denial of pre-plea motions, sentence reasonableness, and an ineffective-assistance claim reserved for collateral review. The order is nonprecedential.

items.summary: The Seventh Circuit affirmed the conviction of Troy D. Burke for bank robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 2113(a) and his 20-year sentence, which was the statutory maximum. Burke argued that the evidence was insufficient, particularly the accuracy of GPS tracking device data tied to marked cash he received from a teller. The court found that testimony from the teller, the credit union president, and the arresting officer, along with photographs and surveillance video, was sufficient for a rational trier of fact to find him guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. The order is nonprecedential.

items.summary: The Seventh Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the defendants in Steven Ingalls, Jr.'s 42 U.S.C. § 1983 action alleging Eighth Amendment deliberate indifference to his medical needs. The defendants were Centurion Health of Indiana, LLC, Dr. Samuel Byrd, and grievance specialist Shelby Crichfield at Wabash Valley Correctional Facility. The court held that the record showed Dr. Byrd exercised medical judgment, that no Centurion policy or practice violation was established, and that Crichfield's rejection of a grievance as untimely did not show deliberate indifference. The order is nonprecedential.

Ludwig, No. 25-3093, the Seventh Circuit issued a nonprecedential order on October 28, 2026, affirming the dismissal of a petition for a writ of mandamus under 28 U.S.C. § 1361 that sought to compel actions by a Chapter 7 bankruptcy trustee. The court held that it had appellate jurisdiction because the unadjudicated Count Three was dismissed during the appeal, and found that the written requirement to report within 72 hours to the nearest probation office after reentry conflicted with the district court's oral pronouncement. items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the bench-trial convictions of Kelvin Patton for Hobbs Act robbery under 18 U.S.C. § 1951 and for brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), along with the 146-month sentence. The court held that the robbery of cash belonging to a Denny's restaurant satisfied the interstate commerce element because the business purchased out-of-state goods, that only a de minimis effect on interstate commerce is required, and that the intended victim's identity was not relevant to that element. The court also held that the denial of a U.S.S.G. § 3E1.1 acceptance-of-responsibility reduction was not without foundation, because the defendant challenged the sufficiency of the evidence on an element of the offense.

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Fifth Circuit affirmed the sentence of Gregory Scott Cook, who pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm by a convicted felon under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(1). Cook raised facial Second Amendment and Commerce Clause challenges to § 922(g)(1) for the first time on appeal, conceded that circuit precedent foreclosed both, and asked the court to hold the appeal in abeyance pending the en banc decision in United States v. Squire. The court declined to hold the appeal, stating that it remains bound by existing precedent absent an intervening Supreme Court or en banc decision, and denied the government's alternative motion for an extension as moot.

items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam opinion filed October 28, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit reviewed the appeal of pro se plaintiff Josue Batista from the Southern District of Florida's dismissal with prejudice of his second amended complaint against Michael Saba, which alleged race discrimination under 42 U.S.C. §§ 1981 and 1982, and from the denial of his Rule 59(e) motion. The court held that the complaint did not plausibly allege intentional race-based discrimination, that the § 1982 claim was properly dismissed and not improperly merged into the § 1981 analysis, and that further amendment would be futile. items.summary: In an unpublished per curiam order, the Eleventh Circuit granted Monsanto Company's unopposed motion for summary affirmance and affirmed a final judgment against it on Nancy Salas's Florida state-law negligent failure-to-warn claim concerning Roundup. The court held that its earlier decision in Carson v. Monsanto Co., 92 F.4th 980 (11th Cir. 2024), controls, concluding that the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) did not preempt the claim. The court reasoned that Florida law, like Georgia law, requires pesticide manufacturers to warn users of potential health and safety risks, paralleling FIFRA.

items.summary: On remand from the Supreme Court, the Eleventh Circuit granted the parties' joint motion for summary adjudication and reversed the district court's judgment against Monsanto Company in the Nancy Salas case. The Supreme Court had granted certiorari, vacated the prior Eleventh Circuit judgment, and remanded for further consideration in light of Monsanto Co. v. Durnell, 609 U.S. 371 (2026). items.opening_verbatim: Public Law 119–135: To convey the reversionary interest of the United States in certain land in Sacramento, California. Public Law 135 Public Law 119–135 140 Stat. 1098 2026-10-22 2026-10-22 United States Government Publishing Office Nation
items.summary: Public Law 119-135, approved October 22, 2026 (H.R. 952), is known as the Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act. It directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Bureau of Land Management, to offer and convey the United States reversionary interest in approximately 8.43 acres in Sacramento, California, to the owner of record of the adjoining parcels within two years of a buyer's request, for not less than fair market value and subject to valid existing rights. The buyer pays the appraised value plus all related costs, and the proceeds are deposited in the Federal Land Disposal Account. The Act also preserves a right-of-way of at least 50 feet on each side of the Southern Pacific Transportation Company main track centerline and does not confirm any adverse possession, prescription, or abandonment claims.
items.title: Public Law 119–135: To convey the reversionary interest of the United States in certain land in Sacramento, California.

items.opening_verbatim: Public Law 119–136: To provide for the transmission of emergency alerts by satellite, and for other purposes. Public Law 136 Public Law 119–136 140 Stat. 1101 2026-10-22 2026-10-22 United States Government Publishing Office National Archive
items.summary: Public Law 119-136, approved October 22, 2026 (H.R. 7022), is known as the Mystic Alerts Act. It requires covered commercial mobile service providers to file an election with the Federal Communications Commission on whether they will transmit emergency alerts by satellite, and sets deadlines for the Commission to publish a notice of proposed rulemaking within 6 months and a final rule within 18 months, in consultation with the Department of Homeland Security and FEMA. The Act sets the rule's effective date as the later of 36 months after Federal Register publication or 12 months after DHS and FEMA implement the necessary alert-origination standards, and prohibits providers from imposing a separate charge for satellite alert transmission. It also limits liability for covered providers that transmit satellite alerts and meet the Act's obligations, and defines a covered service provider as one that voluntarily elects to transmit alerts under the Warning, Alert, and Response Network Act and offers satellite voice and data service.
items.title: Public Law 119–136: To provide for the transmission of emergency alerts by satellite, and for other purposes.

items.summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is proposing to approve the State of Tennessee's attainment plan for the Sullivan County Nonattainment Area (Sullivan County Area or Area) for the 2010 Sulfur Dioxide (SO 2 ) National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS). Additionally, the EPA is proposing to determine that the Area has attained the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS and to approve Tennessee's maintenance plan for continued attainment. With these approvals, the EPA is proposing to approve Tennessee's comprehensive source-specific SO 2 permitted limits for two facilities in the Area, other control measures, and provisions for Reasonably Available Control Measures (RACM) and Reasonably Available Control Technology (RACT), reasonable further progress (RFP), a modeling demonstration of SO 2 attainment and maintenance, and to approve Tennessee's request to redesignate the Area from nonattainment to attainment of the 2010 SO 2 NAAQS. The EPA is taking these actions in accordance with the Clean Air Act (CAA or Act).
items.title: Air Plan Approval and Air Quality Designation; TN; Attainment Plan and Redesignation of the Sullivan County Nonattainment Area for the 2010 1-Hour Primary SO 2 NAAQS

items.opening_verbatim: ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY 40 CFR Part 60 [EPA-HQ-OAR-2025-0163; FRL-12726-01-OAR] RIN 2060-AW73 Additional Reconsideration Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sou
items.summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing amendments to the New Source Performance Standards and Emission Guidelines for the Crude Oil and Natural Gas Source Category to address additional concerns raised with prior regulatory amendments finalized in March 2024. Specifically, the EPA is proposing changes in response to certain petitions for reconsideration of the March 2024 amendments, changes based on policy decisions and supporting legal interpretations, and changes that correct and clarify the regulatory text of the new source performance standards and emission guidelines. First, the EPA proposes to rescind the Super Emitter Program. Second, the EPA proposes to subcategorize different types of well sites affected and designated facilities to address issues related to the requirements finalized in March 2024 for marginal well sites and conventional well sites. Third, the EPA proposes changes to address issues related to liquids unloading, process controllers, pumps, fugitive emissions, storage vessels, covers and closed vent systems, equipment leaks at gas plants, and associated gas. [official summary truncated; see source]
items.title: Additional Reconsideration Standards of Performance for New, Reconstructed, and Modified Sources and Emissions Guidelines for Existing Sources: Oil and Natural Gas Sector Climate Review

items.summary: The Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS) published an interim final rule on August 4, 2026, and republished on August 28, 2026, that amended its arbitration services regulations to clarify when the Office of Arbitration may decline to issue an arbitration panel, make a direct appointment, or provide related services. This document responds to the comments, clarifies the scope of the rule's threshold inquiry, adds procedural provisions governing notice, written disposition, request dates, and fees, and adopts the interim final rule as a final rule.

items.summary: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or the Agency) has received a complete Underground Injection Control (UIC) application from the State of Alaska, requesting primary enforcement responsibility (primacy) for Class VI injection wells under Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) section 1422. The EPA's approval of the State's UIC program primacy application would allow the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation Commission (AOGCC) to issue and enforce compliance with UIC Class VI permits for injection wells used for geologic carbon sequestration. In this action, the EPA proposes to approve Alaska's application to implement the UIC program for Class VI injection wells located within the State, except those located within Indian country and those located within areas of exclusive Federal jurisdiction.
items.title: Alaska Underground Injection Control (UIC) Program; Class VI Primacy

items.summary: This document amends U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) regulations by adding the Republic of Malta (Malta) to the list of countries whose pleasure vessels may be issued U.S. cruising licenses. The U.S. Department of State has notified CBP that yachts used and employed exclusively as pleasure vessels and belonging to any resident of the United States are allowed to arrive at and depart from Maltese ports, and to cruise in Maltese waters without complying with formal entry and clearance procedures. Therefore, CBP is extending reciprocal cruising privileges to Maltese-flagged pleasure vessels.

items.summary: ACF proposes to amend its block grant regulations to modernize requirements, reduce administrative burden on States and Tribal grantees, and improve the clarity and efficiency of program administration. The current regulations include outdated provisions and procedural requirements that no longer reflect statutory authority or agency practice. The proposed revisions are intended to streamline grantee obligations, eliminate unnecessary requirements, and align the regulations with current law and policy.
